strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning three distinct experimental/optimization modalities (NMR NOE restraints, X-ray crystallographic densities, and ipTM confidence scores), with results reported across 20 NMR structures and 13+ X-ray targets rather than a handful of cherry-picked cases, plus extensive supplementary tables (Tables 3-22) supporting the main claims.

The core idea of shifting guidance from coordinate space to the Pairformer conditioning embeddings is a well-motivated and technically sound way to decouple experimental conditioning from the fixed denoising schedule, addressing a genuine limitation of prior guidance-based approaches (Maddipatla et al.).

Strong practical finding: ipTM (and pTM/ipSAE) can be inflated via minute (~0.01%) embedding perturbations without corresponding gains in structural accuracy (Figures 7, 9, 10, 13), which is a valuable and actionable caution for the binder-design/AF3 confidence-metric community.

Reasonably thorough ablations and robustness checks (hyperparameter sensitivity in Table 8, annealing/smoothing/temperature ablation in Table 9, restraint sparsity robustness in Table 10, seed variability in Figure 15, and model-agnosticism demonstrated with Boltz-2 in Figure 14), which aid reproducibility.

Energy-weighted (Boltzmann) reweighting is a principled addition that improves thermodynamic plausibility (lower AMBER/EBM energy, higher ESS) while largely preserving or improving experimental agreement.
Detailed implementation and hyperparameter documentation (Appendix C) supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The compute-normalized comparison in Table 20 shows that at matched denoiser-call budgets (~200 calls) IT-Opt is comparable to or slightly worse than standard guidance, with IT-Opt's advantage only emerging after using up to 4x more denoiser calls (Table 19). This somewhat undercuts the abstract's claim of 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art guidance' and the framing that the method 'eliminates dependence on diffusion length,' since superior results still require substantially larger compute budgets.

The theoretical convergence analysis (Appendix B) rests on several convenient assumptions (local rather than global Lipschitz smoothness justified post hoc by clipping/prior confinement, an unquantified Fisher-information-based bias term Bscore, and an assumed-bounded structural variance term Vstruct) that are plausible but not empirically verified; the analysis reads more as a heuristic justification for an admittedly biased (score-term-dropping) gradient estimator than a tight guarantee.

Core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the closely related guidance line of work (Maddipatla et al., 2024/2025a/2025b) from what appears to be overlapping authorship/lineage; the main innovation (embedding-space vs. coordinate-space conditioning) is a natural extension rather than a fundamentally new idea, and MSA/embedding manipulation for AF has precedent (Bryant & Noé, Wayment-Steele et al.).

The ipTM vulnerability analysis, while important, is based on only 7 complexes with qualitative/case-study level analysis (e.g., single examples highlighted for 1YCS and 2LY4), limiting the statistical robustness of claims about how pervasive or predictable this vulnerability is across protein complex space.

Claims of 'often fitting the experimental data better than deposited PDB structures' are notable but raise concerns about potential overfitting to the density/restraint likelihood at inference time; while MolProbity and force-field energy checks are provided as validity controls, more direct comparison to independent orthogonal experimental validation would strengthen this claim.

Most main-text results tables report point estimates without variance/uncertainty (aside from Figure 15's seed-based error bars for a subset of X-ray targets), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported improvements.

The energy-weighted sampling scheme is entirely dependent on the chosen external force field/EBM (ProteinEBM), and while Table 9 ablates some hyperparameters, the sensitivity to the choice of energy model itself (vs. e.g. classical force fields) is only lightly explored on 3 proteins.

The paper is dense and highly appendix-reliant; the main text often summarizes results via forward references to many supplementary tables/figures, which reduces self-containedness and makes independent verification of central claims more effortful.

strengths: The core idea—optimizing AF3's Pairformer conditioning embeddings (representation-space optimization) rather than perturbing coordinates along a fixed diffusion trajectory—is a reasonable and useful generalization of existing experiment-guided diffusion methods, addressing genuine limitations (fixed sampling horizon, initialization sensitivity) of prior coordinate-space guidance approaches.

Broad empirical coverage across three distinct experimental modalities (NOE/NMR, X-ray crystallographic density, and ipTM confidence), with consistent qualitative trends favoring IT-Opt over guidance and unguided AF3 baselines in the reported tables/figures.

Extensive supplementary material, including hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Table 8), ablations over annealing/smoothing/temperature choices (Table 9), restraint-sparsity robustness checks (Table 10), seed-variance comparisons (Figure 15), and a (partial) compute-normalized comparison against guidance (Table 20), which show some effort toward rigor and fair comparison.

The ipTM sensitivity analysis is a practically relevant and timely cautionary result for the binder-design community, demonstrating that small embedding perturbations can inflate confidence metrics without corresponding gains in structural accuracy across several interface-level metrics (DockQ, Fnat, ipSAE, H-bond recovery).
The method is shown to generalize across diffusion backbones (AF3/Protenix and Boltz-2, Figure 14), supporting the claim that the approach is largely model-agnostic.
weaknesses: The theoretical convergence analysis (Appendix B) is largely a post-hoc rationalization rather than a rigorous guarantee: the REINFORCE score term is dropped purely for computational tractability, its omission is framed as a 'deliberate choice,' and the resulting bias/variance bounds depend on several unverified or essentially unverifiable quantities (Fisher information trace, local Lipschitz constants, bounded structural variance) that are never estimated or validated empirically, making the 'non-asymptotic' guarantee largely vacuous in practice.

Benchmark sizes are modest (20 NMR structures, 13 X-ray segments mostly short peptides/altloc regions of a handful of residues, 7 ipTM complexes), and no statistical significance testing (confidence intervals, paired tests) is reported to support the claimed 'consistent' superiority across methods beyond visual inspection of violin plots and per-target tables.

The claim that IT-Opt 'often fits experimental data better than deposited PDB structures' is presented largely as a positive result without sufficient scrutiny of whether this reflects genuine improved accuracy versus overfitting to noisy experimental signal (density maps, NOE bounds); the validity-loss regularizer mitigates but does not fully address this interpretive risk.

IT-Opt incurs substantially higher computational cost than standard guidance (Table 19), and the compute-normalized fairness comparison (Table 20) is conducted only on the NMR benchmark, leaving the computational trade-off for X-ray and ipTM settings unaddressed.

The Boltzmann reweighting scheme relies on a separate learned energy model (ProteinEBM) to assess thermodynamic plausibility of another learned generative model's (AF3's) samples, introducing a circularity/compounding-bias concern that is not deeply analyzed beyond a single ablation table on 3 proteins.

The ipTM vulnerability finding, while useful, is somewhat incremental given existing literature already documenting ipTM/confidence-metric limitations (e.g., actifpTM, ipSAE, related benchmarking work cited in Section 6); the paper's contribution here is more a confirmatory case study than a fundamentally new insight.

There is a methodological gap between the stated Bayesian/ELBO formulation (Equations 1-2) and the actual implemented algorithm, which adds several additional heuristic loss terms (validity likelihood, substructure conditioner, energy annealing, EMA smoothing, percentile-based energy biasing) not derived from the stated objective, making the formal problem statement somewhat disconnected from the practical method actually evaluated.

The extensive appendix (contributing roughly 30 pages of additional tables/proofs) raises concerns about whether the core 9-page submission on its own provides sufficient self-contained evidence and rigor, with much of the critical validation relegated to supplementary material.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated methodological contribution: optimizing Pairformer conditioning embeddings (representation-space) rather than coordinate-space guidance addresses genuine limitations of prior experiment-guided diffusion methods (fixed sampling horizon, initialization sensitivity), and is framed cleanly as variational inference with an ELBO-type surrogate.

Broad empirical validation across three distinct modalities (NOE-based NMR, crystallographic electron density, and ipTM confidence), with consistent improvements over multiple strong baselines (AlphaFold3, AlphaFlow, ESMFlow, AFCluster, BioEMU, and prior coordinate-guidance methods) and extensive supplementary tables/ablations (hyperparameter sensitivity, restraint sparsity robustness, annealing/smoothing ablations, MolProbity validity checks, seed-to-seed stability).

The Boltzmann/energy-reweighting scheme is theoretically grounded via a self-normalized importance sampling argument and demonstrably improves energetic plausibility (ESS, AMBER/EBM energy) without requiring additional model training.

The ipTM vulnerability analysis is a valuable and practically important finding: it shows confidence metrics widely used for ranking/design (ipTM, and even newer metrics like ipSAE) can be inflated by tiny embedding perturbations without genuine structural improvement, which has direct implications for binder-design false discovery rates.

Reasonable attempt at compute-fairness via a compute-normalized comparison (matched denoiser-call budgets) and a detailed runtime/memory analysis, and the method is shown to generalize to a different backbone model (Boltz-2), supporting the claim of model-agnosticism.

Substantial effort toward reproducibility: detailed algorithmic pseudocode, hyperparameter settings, dataset curation details, and an extensive (if dense) theoretical convergence analysis of the biased stochastic optimization procedure.
weaknesses: Benchmark scale is modest for the claims made: 20 NMR structures, 13 X-ray fragments, and only 7 complexes for the ipTM sensitivity study; broader, less curated benchmarks (e.g., standard interface-prediction datasets) would strengthen generalizability claims, especially for the ipTM finding which is central to the binder-design implications.

The contributions of embedding optimization versus the final coordinate-space guidance warm-start are somewhat entangled — the paper states that optimized embeddings are used to initialize a subsequent coordinate-guidance step (Section 4, Figure 8), making it harder to isolate how much of the improvement is attributable to representation-space optimization alone versus the downstream refinement.

The theoretical convergence analysis (Appendix B) rests on several strong, not fully verified assumptions (local Lipschitz smoothness confined to a compact region via clipping/prior, boundedness of Fisher information trace) and explicitly discards the REINFORCE score term as a source of bias without empirically quantifying this bias; the practical relevance of the O(1/K) near-stationarity guarantee to the reported empirical gains is not demonstrated.

IT-Opt requires substantially greater compute (memory and wall-clock, per Table 19) than coordinate-guidance baselines; while a compute-normalized comparison is provided (Table 20), it compares single-run guidance against an outer-loop procedure with carried-over embeddings, and it is unclear whether simply running guidance with more restarts/seeds and selecting the best would close the gap.

Claims of "often fitting the experimental data better than deposited PDB structures" warrant caution, since the likelihood terms used here (L1 density agreement, NOE bound violations) are simplified relative to full crystallographic/NMR refinement pipelines that incorporate additional geometric and resolution-dependent restraints; better agreement with the chosen proxy objective does not necessarily imply a more physically/biologically correct structure.

Presentation is dense, with many overlapping notations, nested algorithms, and cross-referenced appendix tables/figures, which may hinder readability and make it harder for readers to verify specific claims without extensive cross-checking.

The energy-reweighting scheme's reliance on a single force-field/energy model (ProteinEBM, with AMBER99SB as secondary) is not extensively validated against alternative energy functions, raising some concern about sensitivity of the thermodynamic plausibility claims to the specific choice of energy model.
